course.title: Championing Women in Leadership - Thriving Together

items.paragraph: We’ve discussed attitude, authenticity, growth, communication, negotiation, and burnout. One final step to longevity as a female leader is to create a strong support system from female colleagues around you. Like anything else in life, the road to leadership is easier when you’re surrounded by an encouraging tribe. These aren’t just any female colleagues, but the ones you want to emulate, the ones who set the bar.

items.paragraph: There are several types of players you want on your support team, and we’ll go over a few below.

items.title: The Support Team
items.description:
There are several types of players you want on your support team. Here's a few:

  • Work BFFs

  • Comrade-in-arms 

  • Coaches

  • Mentors

items.title: Summary
items.description: These are just a few examples of the great foundations to build your Championing Team.

items.title: Work BFFs
items.description: Work BFFs, if you will, are the unsung heroes of the daily grind. They're the ones who understand your coffee addiction and can read your facial expressions during meetings. These people simply make you feel better! They can be a refreshing break in your weekly routine, giving you the energy to keep going. So don’t skip out on making friends or lunch buddies at work—just make sure they are the type of positive and professional friend who will keep you moving forward.

items.title: Comrade-in-arms
items.description:
Comrade-in-arms are important peers who share similar professional goals or who are your partners on particular projects. Whether you're planning an ambitious marketing campaign, rolling out a new product, or doing something you’ve never done before, having this type of peer in your tribe makes the journey more enjoyable. Comrade-in-arms help keep you accountable and can offer much-needed support in the trenches. Plus, success is sweeter when celebrated with those who truly get the hustle.


Pat’s comrade-in-arms were undoubtedly two of her assistant coaches Mickie DeMoss and Holly Warlick, whom she considered as good friends. The three were inseparable, and Pat often relied upon them to keep her grounded and in check.

items.title: Coaches
items.description: Coaches are just that—those who may or may not work for your organization, but have a history in the workplace and can offer encouragement. A coach is there to offer support and point out potential potholes in the career road to avoid, which a work BFF or comrade-in-arms may not necessarily see from their vantage point. Think of them as an encourager or cheerleader with an eye for critical thinking.

items.title: Mentors
items.description:
Last, but certainly not least, are mentors. A mentor isn’t a peer or a coach, they’re someone who has gone before you in your industry—maybe even at your own organization or one similar. They’re not here to be a cheerleader, but rather to pass on experience. Imagine you're facing a workplace decision that feels impossible. Or you’re wondering how to navigate a new technology rollout you haven’t used before, and the team isn’t on board. This is where mentors come in. They've been there, done that, and can help you navigate the twists and turns. 

Mentors can be male or female, and balanced leaders usually have both on their support team. Cross-generational mentors in particular bring a unique perspective that younger generations might readily miss. A mentor might have prior experience in a role or a particular skill set to teach that will help move you forward in your career path. It's not about finding a friend, it's about finding someone who's been through the trenches and can offer valuable insight and advice.

items.paragraph:
A mentor is someone you trust, admire and respect who will give you honest and invaluable career advice.

Sample questions you might ask a mentor include:

items.description: What steps did you take to advance in your career, and are there specific skills or experiences you recommend I focus on?
How do you approach setting career goals, and are there specific milestones you recommend I aim for in my current role and beyond?
How did you build and leverage your professional network throughout your career? Any tips for effective networking?
As a successful professional, how have you managed to maintain a healthy work-life balance, and do you have any advice for finding that balance?
What strategies do you use for continuous professional development? Can you provide feedback on my current performance and suggest areas where I can improve?

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph:
These are just a few. The sky’s the limit as to how much gold you can mine for with a mentor. If they’re female, for example, you may ask them, "Have you faced gender-related challenges in your career, and if so, how did you overcome them? Any advice for navigating gender bias in the workplace?" 

If they hold/held a position of senior leadership you might ask, "What leadership skills do you believe are essential for success in our industry today and how can I strengthen these skills?" If they are a self-help junkie, ask, “What strategies do you use for continuous professional development?" You get the picture. As one of the first in her industry to smash through the glass ceiling, many colleagues and team members considered Pat herself to be a mentor.

items.paragraph:
Now, mentors aside, let's talk about two words that may make you inwardly cringe: peer review. The beauty of having a tribe is that you now have people you trust in the trenches with you. They can give you not just support but also honest feedback, while a mentor may not witness your daily performance. 

Strong female leaders know not to be afraid of criticism or critique but to seek it out in strategic cases. It's not about judgment; it's about growth.

items.description: What are some overall areas I can improve on?
What is my personal brand? What am I known for?
Are there any relationships I need to improve/work on?
How are my communication skills? Is there anything I need to change?

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph: Listen to what they say! Resilient leaders learn to see feedback as a tool for improvement, not a red mark on their report card.

items.heading: Deep Dive: How to Receive Feedback
items.paragraph: When we show up to the present moment with all of our senses, we invite the world to fill us with joy. The pains of the past are behind us. The future has yet to unfold. But the now is full of beauty simply waiting for our attention.

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph: Finally, but not to be missed, learn to intentionally celebrate the victories of other women in the workplace and have an abundance mindset. Eliminate the scarcity mentality that might propel you to view other women as rivals for a limited number of positions. Other women aren’t competition at work; they can be allies, if you let them. There are several ways to rally around your fellow sisters in the workplace:

back.description: Do they know of a good mixer or networking opportunity in your area? Where do they meet other people in your industry? Did you just have a great experience at a recent conference you’d recommend? Share the knowledge!

Are you a whiz at design or excel spreadsheets? Know someone who is struggling in an area you can help with, or vice versa? Consider a monthly lunch or skill swap to help educate fellow women in the workplace.
Did someone just hit a huge milestone or work anniversary? How about a major promotion? Take a moment to help them celebrate! Victories at work are more meaningful when they’re shared.

Maybe someone you know just went through a hard season at work. Or maybe you’re facing a new software rollout or department reorganization and know someone a floor over who went through the same thing. Ask for advice, and also pass along your own wisdom.
Look for ways to encourage your organization’s support for women in the workplace, from hiring to mentorship programs or peer group committees.

Know of a job posting at your organization that’s the perfect fit for a woman you know? Refer her! How about someone who would be a great candidate for a particular committee? Offer the recommendation!

items.heading: Give Back
items.paragraph: In summary, as you build your tribe and support system at work, be on the lookout for ways to give back. There are people who have helped you get to where you are today, or are mentoring you as a female leader. Take a minute to think about how you can pay it forward with your own talents and skills.

Be the cheerleader someone else needs. Be the resource someone else can count on. Who can you be a reference for, or who needs an introduction? Pat would be the first to reinforce the power of the team in achieving any goal, as opposed to being a lone ranger or individual performer in your career. Remember the old African proverb, “If you want to go fast, go alone. If you want to go far, go together.”

items.heading: Remembering Pat: Everyone Needs Mentorship
items.paragraph: Pat was a mentor to countless young women in her field. Listen to UT Athletic Director Emeritus Joan Cronan explain why everyone needs mentorship, and the importance of being coachable, even as a coach.
Refer to your workbook for the following questions and reflections.
Do you have a mentor in your current profession? List at least two individuals who you feel have mentored you in the past (formally or informally).
Who might you ask to be an additional mentor in your current role? List at least three potential candidates.
What specific questions would you like to ask a mentor?
In the workplace, who is your biggest cheerleader?
What three questions would you like to ask in a peer review?
What top workplace skills do you have that you could share with your female network?
